Utu-Hengal’s successor, Ur-Nammu, despite his mysterious rise to power, turned out to be a brilliant administrator and builder, raising great ziggurats and overseeing the legal and civic reforms that defined this final flowering.

The Guti had retreated to the mountains and resumed their nomadic ways, yet they remained a persistent threat to Sumerian towns—raiding cities and stealing cattle just as they always had. Putting an end to those raids became the driving focus of King Ur-Nammu’s reign. He raised an army and marched into Gutium, determined to break the Gutian threat once and for all. Instead, he was killed in one of the classic Gutian ambushes in the mountain passes.

The death of this last great builder-king triggered the final downward spiral of Sumerian culture. The loss of so beloved a ruler was commemorated in a lengthy epic known as The Death of Ur-Nammu:

“He who was beloved by the troops could not raise his neck anymore. The wise one lay down. Silence descended, as he, who was the vigor of the land, had fallen. The land becomes demolished like a mountain. Like a cypress forest, it was stripped, its appearance changed.”

Ur-Nammu’s death in battle in 2094 BCE shocked the empire and inspired one of Sumer’s most poignant royal elegies.

The poem follows Ur-Nammu as he descends into the underworld and presents his offerings to the gods who dwell there. From the afterlife, the epic places a final, heartbroken lament on the king’s lips:

“Now just as the rain pouring down from heaven cannot turn back, I can never return to see the beautiful bricks of Ur.”

Drought, Famine, and the Martu Wall

Ur-Nammu was killed in the Gutian ambush in 2094 BCE, and four Sumerian kings would follow him on the throne. His immediate successor, King Shulgi, enjoyed real success on the battlefield and reformed the economy as thoroughly as he could. Yet the reigns of the kings who followed him were haunted by unrelenting pressure from the wild mountain regions.

The drought was still biting hard, and the irrigated farmland was growing steadily choked by accumulating layers of salt. As harvests shrank and food grew scarce, more and more nomadic groups were driven to raiding and plundering simply to survive. By now, the Guti were not the only nomadic tribe who threatened the borders of Sumer.

Driven southward by drought and hunger, the Semitic-speaking Martu emerged as the most formidable nomadic threat on Sumer’s western frontier.

One group in particular, known as the Martu, posed the gravest danger. The Martu were Semitic-speaking, sheep-herding nomads from the highlands of Syria and Lebanon. Much as they had viewed the Guti, the Sumerians regarded the Martu as wild and barbarous, describing them in terms steeped in contempt and dread:

“The hostile Martu have entered the plains. The Martu, a ravaging people with canine instinct, like wolves.”

“The Martu, the powerful south wind, who from the remote past have not known cities. The Martu, who know no grain. The Martu, who know no house or town. The savages of the mountains, the Martu who eat raw meat, who are not buried after their death.”

It is clear that by this time, the Martu were finding their nomadic way of life in the Syrian highlands increasingly unsustainable. Relentless drought and famine were pushing them south—out of the arid hills and into the rich farmland of the river valley, straight into Sumer. Despite its waning strength, the Sumerian state remained determined to hold back the Martu incursions. The new king, Shu-Sin, who came after Shulgi’s line, even ordered the construction of a colossal wall stretching between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers.

Building such a barrier was an extraordinary feat of engineering, proving that even in its twilight years, the Sumerian state could still mobilize immense manpower and organizational energy. Known as the Martu Wall, it ran roughly three hundred kilometers long—more than twice the length of Hadrian’s Wall in Britain. Archaeologists have never been able to locate its physical remains, so we can only guess what form it took. Yet its strategic vision is unmistakable: the Martu Wall aimed to turn the fertile plains between the Tigris and the Euphrates into an island fortress—a river on either flank, the sea to the south, and a great fortified wall to the north.

Still, like every wall in history, the Martu Wall was only as strong as the garrison constantly manning it. As the weakened Sumerian state lost the capacity to hold the line, the barrier was bound to fail. In the end, raising that wall was not an act of imperial confidence, but the desperate last resort of an empire caving in on itself. Walls work only until the invaders build bigger ladders.

Ibbi-Sin and the Sack of Ur

The last Sumerian king was a man named Ibbi-Sin, who took the throne in 2028 BCE. Almost as soon as he was crowned, the empire began to fracture. In the very first year of his reign, the eastern city of Eshnunna broke free from imperial control.

Early in Ibbi-Sin’s reign, vassal cities from Eshnunna to Susa broke away, leaving Ur isolated against mounting external pressure.

An even larger rebellion erupted in the third year of his reign, when the city of Susa, in the region of Elam, successfully threw off Ur’s rule. These Elamites—people of the Iranian lowlands—had lived under Sumerian domination and were now beginning to flex their own military muscle. Their resurgence would soon sound the death knell of the Sumerian Age.

The unraveling empire could no longer sustain its defenses along the Martu Wall. In the fifth year of Ibbi-Sin’s reign, the great barrier built by his predecessors gave way. The Martu poured across the frontier and overran the rich farmlands behind it. The consequences were immediate and catastrophic. Food shortages swept the realm; by the seventh and eighth years of his reign, grain prices had surged as much as sixty-fold. Famine struck the capital hardest of all, and people starved to death in the streets of Ur.

Caught between invading armies and spreading starvation, Ibbi-Sin spiraled into panic. One remarkable letter written by his general, Ishbi-Erra, still survives today. Sent to buy grain from the city of Isin, Ishbi-Erra wrote back to his king with a stark, firsthand glimpse of a society coming apart at the seams:

“You ordered me to travel to Isin and Kazallu to purchase grain. With grain reaching the exchange rate of one shekel of silver per gur, 20 talents of silver have been invested in the purchase. But I have heard news that the hostile Martu have entered inside your territories. I entered with the entire amount of grain, and now I have let the Martu, all of them, penetrate inside the land. Because of the Martu, I am unable to hand over this grain for threshing. They are stronger than me, while I am condemned to sitting around.”

The Akkadian general Ishbi-Erra had no intention of returning to the starving capital. Soon he abandoned King Ibbi-Sin altogether, carving out his own realm and declaring himself king of Isin and Nippur. Besieged from every direction, Ibbi-Sin threw himself into a frantic series of last-ditch measures. He reinforced the fortifications of Ur and Nippur, but none of it could stop the tide. Piece by piece, city by city, the Sumerian Empire dissolved until only Ur itself remained standing, ringed by hostile forces.

Before long, the people of Elam—former subjects of Sumer from the foothills of Iran—marched down along the mountain paths with a coalition of tribesmen and laid siege to the great city of Ur. Ibbi-Sin made one final, desperate gamble to repel them, appealing even to the traitor Ishbi-Erra and the hostile Martu for help, but it came to nothing. The Elamites breached the walls of Ur and put the city to the torch. They stormed into the sacred precincts and the ziggurat, slaughtering priests and plundering treasures as they went.

Elamite armies breached Ur’s defenses around 2000 BCE, burning its temples, poisoning its canals, and carrying the last Sumerian king away in chains.

The surrounding fields were torched, and the waterways became fouled with disease. Elamite soldiers broke into the royal palace and seized Ibbi-Sin. They bound him in chains, marched him back across the border to their homeland, and locked him away. He was the last king of Sumer—a civilization that had endured for more than three thousand years. Ibbi-Sin would die in chains, a prisoner of his enemies in a foreign land.

A Post-Sumerian World and a Sacred Dead Language

The fall of Ur stands as one of history’s defining watersheds. It ended the era of a unified Sumerian state and plunged southern Mesopotamia into a fragmented age in which rival city-states scrambled to control the ruins of the old empire. Meanwhile, the drought dragged on, and the salt-choked fields refused to yield barley. Facing hunger and ruin, the Sumerian people began fleeing their homeland in huge numbers, carrying what meager belongings they could—along with their laments for the great fallen cities.

Over the centuries that followed, a vast migration unfolded from southern Mesopotamia toward the north. Many Sumerian speakers settled in Akkadian lands, soon joined by the Martu, who were themselves settling down inside the cities they had overrun. Fleeing Sumerians, migrating Martu, and native Akkadians mingled together, blending their traditions just as the peoples of this river valley had always done. From that cultural fusion rose the next great chapter of Mesopotamian history—and the region’s new superpowers, the Babylonian and Assyrian empires.

Sumerian itself was now a dead language. It would never again be heard in bustling streets or noisy markets, and gradually it faded from everyday memory. Yet it survived inside the temples, much as medieval European churches preserved Latin long after the fall of Rome. Later Mesopotamian rulers kept Sumerian alive in their shrines and scriptures for at least another two thousand years. To these later generations, Sumerian became the language of the gods, and the ancient kings of Ur and Uruk passed into legend—some even revered as gods themselves.

For the next two millennia, every great king of Mesopotamia, whether in Babylon or Assyria, claimed legitimacy under a single resonant title—King of Sumer and Akkad—reaching back to the first age, the dawn of humanity’s journey into civilization.

When the Rivers Left: The Slow Death of Ur

Even after the collapse of the Sumerian Empire, Ur did not vanish overnight. It endured as a population center, rising and falling several times over the centuries of the post-Sumerian era.

In the end, however, it was the landscape that had given birth to Ur, and it was the landscape that sealed its fate. Today, the Persian Gulf that once nourished Ur’s harbors lies nowhere near its ruins. When archaeologists unearthed Ur in 1815 CE, deep in the desert, they were astonished to find millions of seashells scattered across the site. Over the millennia, the steady buildup of river silt—combined with shifting global sea levels—pushed Iraq’s gulf coastline far back to its present edge, roughly one hundred kilometers south of Ur.

Once a thriving port near the Persian Gulf and the Euphrates, Ur now sits surrounded by arid desert—about a hundred kilometers from the modern coast.

The Euphrates River, which had once carried the bounties of northern trade straight to Ur’s quays, also abandoned the city, shifting its channel over the centuries. Today, nothing surrounds the ruins except miles of arid desert. Water had always been Ur’s lifeblood; losing both the sea and the river condemned the city to a slow, quiet death.

Gradually, people left its houses and lanes behind. They stopped tending the fields and clearing the irrigation canals; the earth cracked dry, and the fertile topsoil blew away on the wind. Priests extinguished the sacred fire in the upper chamber of the ziggurat and ceased bringing offerings to the moon god, Sin. The markets shut down, mudbrick walls crumbled, and timber roof beams rotted and collapsed.

Desert winds and drifting sand rolled through the empty streets, and dunes buried the fallen ramparts. Before long, the greatest city the early world had ever known was reduced to a lonely mound of earth, passed only by the occasional desert traveler. It was among these very ruins that the Italian traveler Pietro Della Valle once took shelter with his wife while hiding from bandits—and through him that Europe first glimpsed the scattered fragments of writing the Sumerians had left behind in their forgotten script. Somewhere beneath the silent mounds of Ur lay the clay tablets bearing The Lament for Ur:

“May that storm swoop down no more on your city. May the door be closed on it like the great city gate at nighttime. Until distant days, other days, future days. In your city reduced to ruin mounds may a lament be made to you. Oh Nanna, may your restored city be resplendent before you.”

Desert Mounds and the Voices That Survived in Clay

Following the sack of Ur around 2000 BCE, the ancient metropolis of Uruk also fell into steep decline, and much of its population fled. Uruk did enjoy a later revival when it served as a regional capital under the Assyrian Empire. Yet when the Euphrates shifted its course there too, Uruk was abandoned completely.

The eroded walls of Uruk—immortalized in The Epic of Gilgamesh—still rise fifteen meters above the desert floor, littered with ancient potsherds.

Even today, the walls of Uruk—the very walls celebrated so vividly in The Epic of Gilgamesh—remain visible. Long ridges of ancient brickwork trace a flat, lunar desert landscape, still rising fifteen meters high around a city washed by a quiet tide of broken pottery and bleached bones. The English archaeologist William Loftus was the first European to reach Uruk. When he came upon its ruins in 1849 CE, he was struck by the haunting sight of those immense mounds rising from the wilderness, later writing: “Of all the desolate sights I ever beheld, that of Uruk incomparably surpasses all.”

Across all the ancient cities of Sumer—in Nippur and Eridu, in Kish and Lagash, in Ur and Uruk—decay was gradual, yet unstoppable. Windborne sand banked up against standing walls and swallowed the streets; rain and gusts wore down every remaining edifice. The wandering travelers who stumbled across those solitary ruins must have traded quiet stories about what could have happened to the people who built such staggering monuments and then vanished from the earth.

With their cities in ruins, the Sumerians slipped out of living history. Even the empires that succeeded them—the ones that kept Sumerian alive in their temples and retold tales of its kings—eventually crumbled into ruin themselves. The knowledge of how to read Sumerian was lost, and its history turned to dust. Only the clay tablets endured, sleeping beneath the sands of southern Iraq—fragile vessels holding the voices of an entire people, waiting for archaeologists to unearth them and, through arduous, painstaking scholarship, learn to read them once again.

Buried beneath desert sand for millennia, Sumerian clay tablets preserve everything from grain ledgers and recipes to timeless meditations on mortality.

Those fragments send us sudden bursts of light from the most distant human past. They preserve the Sumerians’ ledgers and recipes, their music and prayers, their loves and griefs, their triumphs and their heartbreaking laments for the world’s first cities. And they preserve the wistful philosophy of those earliest writers, captured in lines from The Epic of Gilgamesh:

“Nobody sees death. Nobody sees the face of death. Nobody hears the voice of death. Savage death just cuts mankind down. Sometimes we build a house, sometimes we make a nest, but then brothers divide it upon inheritance. Sometimes, there is hostility in the land, but the river rises and brings floodwater. Dragonflies drift on the river, their faces look upon the face of the sun, but then suddenly there is nothing.”

Outlived by the Woolly Mammoths

Before I bring this series to a close, I want to return one last time to the woolly mammoths. When the Sumerians first reached Iraq’s southern coast around 5500 BCE, the very last woolly mammoths on earth were fighting for survival on the opposite side of the planet.

They had made Wrangel Island their final refuge and clung to existence there, even as the Sumerians were sowing the seeds of humanity’s first civilization in southern Iraq. On that small, rocky island on the rim of the Arctic Ocean, the last woolly mammoths finally lay down and died around 1700 BCE—at a time when the last kings of Ur were already a distant memory.

Sumerian society, in its imperial form, had risen, lived out its golden age for more than three thousand years, and passed into silence—outlived by the woolly mammoth.

title: Sumer Rises Again: The Gutian Dark Age and the Ur III Renaissance
body:
From the Hale-Bopp omen and the Gutian dark age to Ur-Nammu's ziggurats and the salt that choked the fertile earth.

When the great Akkadian king Naram-Sin died in 2218 BCE, his son Shar-Kali-Sharri inherited not only a gilded throne, but an empire already fraying at the edges. In the fourth year of his reign, an unforgettable sign blazed across the Mesopotamian night. Nearly two hundred million kilometers away, a frozen wanderer—forty kilometers wide, a ball of ancient ice and dust—swept close enough to burn like a torch in the heavens.

Within a single generation, that skyward omen would seem eerily prophetic. A global climate shock, a centuries-long drought, and nomadic raiders from the northern hills would erase Sargon's proud capital from the map—yet out of that century and a half of ruin, Sumer itself would rise one last time for a luminous, final golden age.

In short

  • Comet Hale-Bopp blazed over Mesopotamia in 2213 BCE—just as the global 4.2-kiloyear drought struck Egypt, the Indus Valley, China's Liangzhu culture, and Akkad.
  • Starved and fractured by civil war, the Akkadian Empire fell to the nomadic Guti, who burned Akkad beyond trace and presided over a 150-year dark age.
  • Utu-Hengal of Uruk expelled the Guti and restored Sumerian kingship, paving the way for Ur-Nammu's Third Dynasty of Ur—the Neo-Sumerian Renaissance.
  • Ur-Nammu codified the earliest surviving law code, standardized silver currency, and crowned Sumer with towering white ziggurats, even as creeping soil salinity slowly choked the valley's farmlands.

Hale-Bopp: The Lonely Cosmic Traveler

Comet Hale-Bopp appeared over Mesopotamia in 2213 BCE and returned more than four millennia later in 1997.

This visitor was Comet Hale-Bopp, appearing in Earth's sky for the first time in 2213 BCE. It would spend the next four millennia plunging through the outer reaches of our solar system in a deep elliptical orbit before returning past Earth as a blazing streak of light in 1997.

In that modern return, Hale-Bopp became the brightest comet in living memory. For eighteen months it hung visible in our night skies, its glowing tail stretched across the stars, dazzling millions. Yet awe was not its only legacy.

In March 1997, thirty-nine members of an apocalyptic cult called Heaven's Gate took their own lives. Wearing matching Nike "Just Do It" sneakers, they drank a lethal mix of vodka and phenobarbital and lay down together, convinced their souls would be lifted aboard a spaceship hidden behind the comet's iridescent tail.

If a ball of ice and dust could inspire such fevered belief at the close of the twentieth century, we can only imagine the fears and omens it stirred in the minds of ancient Mesopotamians. Some may have read a divine blessing in its radiant arc; others saw a solitary herald of catastrophe. In time, it was the darker reading that proved tragically right.

The 4.2-Kiloyear Event: When the World's Climate Shifted

During the reign of King Shar-Kali-Sharri, Earth's climate underwent a sudden and mysterious shift. Today, paleoclimatologists give it a terse, clinical name: the 4.2-kiloyear event (4.2 ka event). Scholars have tentatively linked it to shifts in North Atlantic sea ice that rippled outward through the planet's delicate, intimately connected climate system, disrupting atmospheric circulation and sharply cutting rainfall across vast swaths of the globe.

This sudden shift—and the punishing drought that followed—is tied to civilizational collapses across the ancient world. Egypt's Old Kingdom withered. The Indus Valley civilization contracted. The Liangzhu culture in China collapsed. And in Mesopotamia, the rains withdrew, the earth baked hard, and the two rivers that had nourished empires for millennia no longer rose with their old generosity.

This dry spell was no brief bad season; it lingered for well over a century—some researchers argue as long as three centuries. Studies of Mesopotamian dust layers confirm that annual rainfall plunged dramatically while the climate turned sharply more arid. The seasonal river floods on which regional agriculture depended began to fail routinely, and famine crept across the plains.

Inside the Akkadian Empire, vital resources grew scarce. The age of booming grain surpluses was over, and the first towns and cities began to be abandoned across the drier northern plains. When King Shar-Kali-Sharri died in 2193 BCE, the empire collapsed into bitter civil war and chaos. The Sumerian King List records the ensuing breakdown with dry, biting sarcasm:

"Then who was king? Who was not king? Four of them ruled in only three years."

The Gutian Period: A Miniature Dark Age in Mesopotamia

All this unraveling did not go unnoticed. Up in the northern mountains overlooking the Mesopotamian plains, a nomadic tribal people watched as the mighty Akkadian Empire tore itself apart. These were the Guti.

Who the Guti were, what tongue they spoke, and which gods they revered remain largely shrouded in mystery. What survives is the unmistakable contempt preserved in Sumerian and Akkadian texts:

"The Guti were an unhappy people, unaware of how to revere the gods and ignorant of right religious practices."

For years, the Guti had raided and plundered along the Akkadian frontier—torching villages and driving off cattle. From their highland ridges, these hill tribes had watched drought hollow out the settled river-valley societies, watching city dwellers fight over shrinking farmland even as they themselves struggled to survive in the parched hills.

Driven by the same regional aridity, the highland Guti descended into Mesopotamia not merely to raid, but to conquer.

At this hour of acute hardship, the Guti gathered their strength and marched down from the mountains into the lands of Sumer—this time not simply to raid, but to claim the valley for themselves. To the stunned peoples of Mesopotamia, the invasion felt like divine wrath from Enlil himself. One extraordinary lament from the era, The Curse of Akkad, captures the terror of the Gutian onslaught:

"Enlil—what destruction he wrought! He raised his eyes to the mountain and mustered the whole mountain as one: the rebellious people, the land whose people are without number—Gutium, that land that brooks no control, whose understanding is human, yet whose appearance and stuttering words are those of a dog. Enlil brought them down from the mountain in vast numbers. Like locusts, they covered the earth. Nothing escaped their arm; no one escaped their arm. All the lands raised a bitter cry on the city walls."

The Guti swiftly overwhelmed the weakened Akkadian defenses. Even before the full invasion, they had mastered hit-and-run warfare—severing supply lines and leaving charred towns in their wake. Their raids shattered Akkad's fragile economy, and the already starving society began to buckle. When the demoralized Akkadian army finally marched out to meet the amassed Guti in open battle, it stood no chance. The Guti swept across the heartland and destroyed Sargon's capital of Akkad so utterly that archaeologists have never located its ruins.

Under Gutian rule, canals silted up, literacy waned, and Mesopotamia endured roughly a century and a half of decline.

For the next hundred and fifty years, the Guti ruled Mesopotamia in misery—a genuine dark age for the river valley. Little writing or art survives from this span, and what has been uncovered looks starkly unsophisticated beside earlier Sumerian and Akkadian craft. The Guti showed scant interest in maintaining canals, keeping written records, or safeguarding public order.

For reasons still unknown, they even rejected keeping livestock in pens and turned domesticated farm animals loose into the wild. Unlettered themselves, the Guti struggled to govern an intricate urban civilization that for over a millennium had depended on the written word. Their neglect deepened the famine, and the valley's hard-won infrastructure steadily crumbled.

Utu-Hengal and the Return of Sumerian Kingship

As resentment toward Gutian rule mounted, sparks of rebellion began to flare across southern Iraq. With the central authority of Akkad gone, several Sumerian city-states quietly reasserted their independence. Soon, one Sumerian leader would step forward to ignite a cultural rebirth—rejecting both Guti and Akkad in a single bold stroke.

Utu-Hengal of Uruk rallied rebel Sumerian cities to drive the Guti out of the river valley.

We know remarkably little about who Utu-Hengal was, only that he served as the Sumerian governor of Uruk—a man who had seen and heard of his homeland reduced to rubble, first under Akkadian domination and then starved under Gutian misrule. Gathering fighters from fellow rebel Sumerian cities, he declared war the moment the last Gutian king, Tirigan, ascended to power. Tirigan had sat on the throne for barely forty days when Utu-Hengal struck.

Before marching into all-out war against the Gutian king, Utu-Hengal turned to the ancient gods of Sumer. He journeyed to the temple of Ishkur, the Sumerian storm god, offered an ancient prayer in the Sumerian tongue, and sacrificed a lamb upon the altar. The Sumerian King List celebrates what happened next:

"Then Tirigan, the king of the Guti, ran away alone on foot. He thought himself safe in Dabrum, where he fled to save his life. But since the people of Dabrum knew that Utu-Hengal was a king endowed with the power of Enlil, the people of Dabrum did not let him go."

"Utu-Hengal made the Guti, the fanged snakes of the mountains, go back to drink again from the rocky crevices of the hills. He brought the kingship back to Sumer."

For the first time since Sargon of Akkad, sovereignty over Mesopotamia returned to Sumerian hands.

Ur-Nammu: The Sumerian Renaissance and the Age of the Ziggurats

After centuries of foreign rule, the Sumerians had finally cast off both Guti and Akkad. For the first time since the days of Sargon, mastery of Mesopotamia rested once again in the hands of a Sumerian king.

Utu-Hengal's triumph ushered in the era historians call the Third Dynasty of Ur—often remembered as the Neo-Sumerian Empire or the Sumerian Renaissance. It was the final flowering of a Sumerian culture already more than three thousand five hundred years old, and its closing act left an indelible mark on all human history that followed.

Yet despite winning kingship back for Sumer, Utu-Hengal did not reign for long. He died under mysterious circumstances—very likely killed by one of his own ambitious governors, a man named Ur-Nammu. However shadowy his path to the throne may have been, Ur-Nammu proved an extraordinary ruler. A brilliant administrator who enacted sweeping reforms, he standardized weights and measures across the marketplaces of his kingdom. He divided silver into a unit called the mina, composed of sixty shekels—laying the groundwork for the world's first standardized currencies centuries later. And he promulgated a written collection of laws that stands today as the earliest surviving legal code in human history, pre-dating the more famous Code of Hammurabi by three full centuries.

Three centuries before Hammurabi, Ur-Nammu codified laws and standardized silver weights across his Neo-Sumerian state.

Beyond law and governance, Ur-Nammu was a prodigious builder. He restored the ancient cities of Nippur, Ur, Larsa, Kish, Adab, and Umma, repairing royal roads and reviving irrigation canals neglected for more than a century under the Guti. Yet above all else, Ur-Nammu loved building ziggurats. Under his patronage, nearly every major Sumerian city gained a ziggurat that served as its towering civic and spiritual centerpiece. Each night it would have glowed bright white beneath the moonlight, just as intended—a monumental shrine raised to the moon god, Sin.

These ziggurats—distinctive stepped towers—represent the hallmark and architectural pinnacle of Sumer. Rising in three terraced tiers like a grand wedding cake, with sweeping staircases ascending to the summit, they were constructed entirely from baked clay bricks bound with bitumen and coated in luminous white gypsum that gleamed under the desert sun. Priests planted trees and flowers along the terraces and lit the topmost shrine with candles after dusk.

The Great Ziggurat of Ur once rose roughly thirty meters high—the height of a modern ten-story building.

The grandest of all these ziggurats stood in Ur-Nammu's home city of Ur. In its heyday it rose roughly thirty meters above the plain—the equivalent of a ten-story building. Nearly four thousand years later, in 1617 CE, the wandering Italian traveler Pietro Della Valle took shelter amid its weathered brick ruins.

Water and Salt: How the Fertile Earth Choked Sumer

Yet even amid this dazzling late renaissance, the very nature that had birthed Sumerian civilization was quietly preparing to swallow its great cities whole.

The waters flowing down the Euphrates and Tigris carried rich silt—along with microscopic traces of dissolved salt and minerals. Because both rivers cut across the limestone-rich Taurus Mountains, they carry higher mineral and salt loads than most great rivers. When ancient farmers channeled this water onto the fields of Sumer, the fierce Mesopotamian sun evaporated the water and left tiny residues of salt behind. During centuries of generous rain, annual downpours and spring floods flushed those salts safely away.

Once the centuries-long arid spell settled in, however, the earth beneath Sumer's feet began to fail. After roughly 2200 BCE, persistent dryness across southern Iraq meant more and more salt stayed trapped in the topsoil. Slowly, relentlessly, salinity crept upward until crops struggled to take root. Because Sumerian scribes meticulously recorded their annual grain harvests, the clay tablets after 2300 BCE paint a starkly grim trajectory.

One unmistakable clue lies in the steady shift from wheat to more salt-tolerant barley as Sumer's primary crop. In the city of Girsu around 3550 BCE, farmers harvested wheat and barley in roughly equal proportions. After a thousand years of continuous irrigation, wheat had fallen to just six percent of the annual yield. By 2000 BCE, wheat accounted for barely two percent—silent, mathematical proof of a soil poisoned by accumulating salt.

Switching to barley in both field and kitchen was a remarkably resourceful adaptation. It is easy to cast the Sumerians as reckless farmers who ruined their land out of greed, yet they actively fought the creeping crisis. Without modern soil science, they still practiced crop rotation, left fields fallow to rest, and dug drainage channels to flush their farmland.

Over centuries of drought and irrigation, salt gradually crusted the topsoil of southern Mesopotamia, forcing farmers from wheat to hardy barley.

For all their ingenuity, the last Sumerians could only slow the tide, never reverse it. As decades turned into centuries and the dry years dragged on, urban populations kept growing while the exhausted fields yielded less and less. Eventually, a white crust of salt coated the topsoil, and almost nothing would grow at all.

The same earth that had once nourished the world's first cities was slowly choking the life out of Sumer. Even so, the final blow to Sumerian civilization would arrive not solely from parched soil, but at the point of a spear. Ur-Nammu himself fell in battle against the Guti, and four successive kings followed him, faithfully carrying forward his reforms.

Yet the relentless drought soon drove another nomadic people down from the northwest—the Martu (Amorites)—triggering the empire's final downward spiral. When the last Sumerian king of Ur, Ibbi-Sin, took the throne in 2028 BCE, his realm began fracturing almost the moment the crown touched his head. And the fatal death knell of Sumerian civilization was already gathering to the east, in the rising power of Elam—a people of southwestern Iran who were only beginning to flex their strength upon the stage of history.

title: Sargon of Akkad: How the Akkadians Took Power in Mesopotamia
body:
How a cupbearer from Kish humbled Sumer, forged Mesopotamia's first empire, and watched a three-century drought undo it.

For centuries, the history of Mesopotamia belonged to the Sumerian city-states of the south—proud, fiercely independent, and endlessly at war over canals, borderlands, and prestige. Yet even at the height of Sumerian ambition, when the conqueror Lugal-zage-si boasted that his dominion stretched from the Persian Gulf to the Mediterranean Sea, another people were quietly waiting in the wings. They were the Akkadians, long treated as the junior partners in the great river-valley civilization.

Out of their ranks would step one man who led them into outright rebellion against Sumerian rule. History remembers him as Sargon—a name that in Akkadian means "the true king." With a single audacious stroke against the walls of Uruk, he would topple the old order, found the world's first true empire, and usher in the long twilight of the Sumerian age.

In short

  • In Sumerian Mesopotamia, holding cities was never enough; true legitimacy required the blessing of Enlil at his sacred seat of Nippur.
  • Lugal-zage-si of Umma unified Sumer and claimed rule "between the seas," but his overstretched empire quickly fractured into rebellion.
  • Sargon, a cupbearer from Kish of humble legend, seized Uruk in a surprise strike, humiliated Lugal-zage-si at Nippur, and founded a new imperial capital at Akkad.
  • Under Sargon and his grandson Naram-Sin, Akkadian displaced Sumerian as the living language of administration and commerce—before a three-century drought and Gutian invasions brought the empire down.

Enlil and Nippur: The Sacred Seat of Sumerian Kingship

In Sumerian legend, three great deities tower over the pantheon: An, the sky father; Enki, the wise lord of the subterranean waters; and Enlil, the god of the "between"—the air, space, and breath where divine authority resides.

During the early centuries of the third millennium BCE, the Sumerians elevated Enlil from a local city deity to the supreme god of Sumerian culture. In this age of Enlil, ruling Sumer meant far more than holding wealthy cities like Uruk or Ur; it meant holding the mandate of Enlil.

Enlil, lord of wind and air, whose blessing at Nippur conferred legitimate kingship across Sumer.

Throughout the fourth millennium BCE, Nippur was never a political powerhouse. Situated along the Euphrates, it was neither the richest nor the most heavily fortified city in the valley, and it never spawned a conquering dynasty of its own. Yet its central geographic position—roughly midway along the Euphrates' course through the heartland—made it accessible to every major city-state. Nippur's authority flowed from a far more enduring source: it was the home of Enlil, and by extension, the spiritual fountainhead of all Sumerian kingship.

The temple of Ekur in Nippur served as Enlil's earthly residence. This was no hollow ceremonial convention; Sumerian inscriptions repeatedly depict victorious kings journeying to Nippur to lay offerings before the god and claim their legitimacy. When Lugal-zage-si marched out of Umma and began subduing rival city-states—Kish, Larsa, Ur, and Uruk—raw military might was not enough. Without Enlil's sanction, his rule would remain incomplete.

Empires rose and crumbled across Mesopotamia, yet Nippur endured as the quiet city where conquerors sought divine sanction.

In the long ebb and flow of Mesopotamian history, Uruk rose, then Ur, then Akkad, then Babylon. Each in turn marched its armies to Nippur, bowed inside the Ekur, and declared itself chosen. Empires came and crumbled; Nippur endured—the quiet city that crowned the mighty and buried their ambitions beneath the sands.

Lugal-zage-si and the Dream of Ruling Between the Seas

The uprising against the hated empire of Lagash had thrust a fierce rebel to the forefront: Lugal-zage-si of Umma. Once he sacked Lagash, his momentum proved unstoppable. Working his way north along the course of the Tigris and Euphrates, he swiftly absorbed every territory Lagash had once claimed—and refused to stop at its old borders.

At the height of his triumphs, Lugal-zage-si even claimed to have conquered all the land between the "upper sea and lower sea"—meaning the Mediterranean Sea and the Persian Gulf. That boast was almost certainly an exaggeration. Up to this point in history, the Sumerians had never managed to hold distant colonies or occupy far-flung lands for long. Yet one royal inscription declares in sweeping terms:

"The great god Enlil gave the kingship of the land to him—the region from the lower sea, through the Tigris and Euphrates, to the upper sea. Thirty-two kings gathered against him, but he defeated them and smote their cities, prostrated their lords, and destroyed the whole countryside as far as the silver mines."

This was the first time a Sumerian prince had ever staked such a claim: king of the land between the seas. To the Sumerians, the upper sea marked the western edge of the known world. Even if Lugal-zage-si's reach fell short of his words, the vision of a single ruler commanding everything between the two seas lingered in the imagination of every ambitious king who followed him.

Like King Eannatum of Lagash before him, however, Lugal-zage-si committed the fatal mistake of overstretching his resources. His newly stitched-together realm was simply too vast to govern cleanly. Before long, civil strife and open rebellion flared across several Sumerian cities.

Sargon of Akkad: The Cupbearer Who Toppled Sumer

Into this season of chaos and instability stepped the other great people of Mesopotamia, finally sensing their moment to rule. Until now, they had lived as the junior partner in the shared river-valley civilization. These were the people of Akkad—and Sargon was the man who would lead them to power.

Sargon of Akkad, whose legend begins not with a crown, but with a reed basket drifting on the Euphrates.

Sargon was not of noble birth; his story does not begin with a crown. His origin legend sounds uncannily familiar to anyone raised on biblical tales. Born in the twenty-fourth century BCE to a humble mother, he was said to have been placed in a reed basket sealed with bitumen and set adrift on the river, only to be fished out and raised by a gardener working at the royal palace of Kish.

Growing up in obscurity, Sargon began his ascent as cupbearer to the king of Kish. In ancient Mesopotamia, that title meant far more than pouring wine. A cupbearer stood at the very elbow of power—trusted with the king's life, listening to counsel, learning the rhythms of court politics and the fractures beneath them. Before long, the king entrusted Sargon with a mission of the utmost secrecy.

At the time, Kish remained under the thumb of Lugal-zage-si's Sumerian empire. The Sumerian emperor was away on a distant campaign, possibly fighting far to the west in the lands of Syria. Young Sargon was handed a small band of fighters and ordered south to Uruk, where Lugal-zage-si kept his royal capital. The plan was bold to the point of recklessness: strike Uruk by surprise, knock out the imperial capital, and break Kish free from Sumerian domination.

The towering walls of Uruk must have looked daunting to Sargon and his men. Yet Lugal-zage-si had taken the bulk of his army on campaign, leaving only a thin garrison behind. The assault caught the defenders completely off guard. Sargon's men overwhelmed the watch, scaled the ramparts, and seized the city. Before reinforcements could arrive, Sargon tore down wide sections of Uruk's mighty walls—a deliberate, deeply symbolic blow aimed at the pride of Sumer.

Lugal-zage-si was furious. He marched back at speed, rallying as many as fifty subject kings according to the inscriptions. On paper, their task looked simple enough: crush the upstart forces of a single rebel city-state. We do not know the exact tactics Sargon used on the field, only the astonishing outcome—in pitched battle, Sargon's army shattered the combined might of the Sumerian empire.

Sargon captured Lugal-zage-si alive and marched him in chains through the gates of the holy city of Nippur. There, before the temple of Enlil, Sargon subjected the fallen emperor to a searing public humiliation, forcing him to wear a wooden neck stock—a heavy yoke clamped around his neck and shoulders.

Victory imagery from the Akkadian era—Sargon humiliated Lugal-zage-si at Nippur, yet remarkably spared his life.

It was a theatrical display of dominance, yet what Sargon did next set him apart from most conquerors of his age. He did not execute the old king. Remarkably, Lugal-zage-si was permitted to live and even continue governing Uruk, provided he swore an oath of loyalty to the new high king, Sargon.

The Rise of Akkad: A New Capital and a New Order

Victory over Lugal-zage-si did not merely close one man's reign—it closed an entire era. With the Sumerian coalition broken and its proudest emperor humbled, Sargon turned to building something altogether unprecedented.

Sargon refused to make Uruk, Kish, or even Nippur his royal seat. Instead, he founded a brand-new capital of his own: the city of Akkad. Akkad was a political declaration—a deliberate break from centuries of Sumerian city-state rivalries. It was a center of power that answered to Sargon of Akkad, rather than to the ancient priesthoods and patron gods of the south.

From this new capital, Sargon marched out to conquer everything his predecessors had claimed, and more. An inscription carved beneath a statue in Nippur boasts:

"Sargon, the king of Kish, triumphed in thirty-four battles over the cities, up to the edge of the seas, and destroyed their walls. He bowed down to the gods, and the gods gave him the upper land—up to the cedar forest and up to the silver mountains."

Sargon also studied the mistakes of earlier conquerors and resolved not to repeat them. Wherever his armies took a city, he made a point of demolishing its defensive walls, stripping conquered populations of the shelter needed to stage a revolt. Once his empire was secure, he performed a grand ritual to proclaim his mastery over the known world: he washed his weapons in the waters of both the Persian Gulf and the Mediterranean Sea.

When the dust of conquest settled, Sargon proved himself an able state-builder. He centralized imperial administration, standardized weights and measures, and reformed the dating system across his realm. In many respects, he looks like a forward-thinking, pragmatic ruler. Yet Sargon was also, by any modern measure, an Akkadian nationalist.

He took a new royal title—King of Akkad—and placed fellow Akkadians in the empire's key offices. For centuries, Sumerian had stood unchallenged as the official language of royal inscriptions on palaces and temples across Mesopotamia. Under Sargon, Akkadian entered official royal inscriptions for the very first time. The ancient cuneiform script was adapted and re-engineered to record the Semitic sounds of Akkadian. Administration shifted steadily into Akkadian, while Sumerian retreated into the sacred sphere of temples, ritual, and scholarship.

The two peoples of Mesopotamia, who had lived, farmed, and built side by side for thousands of years, were beginning to drift apart. In the southern Sumerian-speaking cities, resentment simmered until it reached a boiling point.

Sargon reigned for fifty-five years, and in the twilight of his life that simmering anger exploded into a full-scale uprising. A later Babylonian chronicle preserves the memory:

"In his old age, all the lands revolted against him, and they besieged him in Akkad the city. But he went forth to battle and defeated them. He knocked them over and destroyed their vast armies."

Sargon's sheer flair for war held the empire together as long as he drew breath, yet as the aging monarch weakened, virtually every southern city burst into open revolt. When Sargon died around 2284 BCE, it fell to his two sons to inherit—and somehow contain—the storm he left behind.

The first son, Rimush, ruled for nine bloody years, spending nearly all of them fighting bitter campaigns to reconquer the rebellious Sumerian south. He crushed uprisings in Ur, Umma, Lagash, and Adab; one year of his reign entered history under the grim name "the year that Adab was destroyed." When Rimush died, Sargon's other son, Manishtushu, took the throne, reportedly falling back on the same harsh tactics of terror that had once made the old empire of Lagash so detested.

It took Sargon's grandson, Naram-Sin, to restore the Akkadian Empire to its former brilliance. He quelled the southern heartlands and returned the realm to stability. Yet Naram-Sin understood that force alone could not bind Mesopotamia together. Breaking with his grandfather's narrower title, "King of Akkad," he adopted a more diplomatic style: King of Sumer and Akkad—a deliberate gesture of reconciliation between the two halves of his empire.

A Cosmopolitan Empire and the Twilight of Spoken Sumerian

Still, even Naram-Sin could not fully mend the cultural shift already underway. The Sumerians were no longer the dominant creative engine of the region. For generations, Akkadian had been quietly overtaking Sumerian in the streets and marketplaces. Official imperial preference played its part, of course, but the deeper cause lay in the cosmopolitan makeup of the empire itself.

Sumerian was a language isolate—its grammar, structure, and sounds bore no kinship to any neighboring tongue. By contrast, the peoples living across the surrounding lands spoke languages closely related to Akkadian, all belonging to the wider Semitic language family. They shared similar grammatical roots, familiar patterns, and overlapping vocabulary. For travelers, merchants, and migrants entering Mesopotamia, picking up Akkadian was rather like an English speaker learning French, whereas Sumerian felt altogether alien—more like trying to learn Bengali from scratch.

Re-engineered from Sumerian cuneiform, Akkadian became the natural lingua franca of trade, diplomacy, and empire.

Because Akkadian was so much easier for outsiders to learn, it naturally became the lingua franca of trade, diplomacy, and daily commerce. Mesopotamia had been largely bilingual for centuries, but the balance now tipped decisively. Gradually, every Sumerian had to learn Akkadian, while fewer and fewer Akkadians saw any need to learn Sumerian.

Slowly, quietly, spoken Sumerian began to slip out of living history. Priests and scholars would preserve it inside temples and ziggurats as a sacred tongue of liturgy and learning for another two thousand years—much as Latin endured in medieval Europe—but its days as a spoken mother tongue were drawing to a close.

A Lonely Comet, a Great Drought, and the Fall of Akkad

Yet the days of the Akkadian Empire were numbered as well. When the great Naram-Sin died, the throne passed to his son, Shar-Kali-Sharri—the great-grandson of Sargon of Akkad. In the fourth year of his reign, a lonely cosmic traveler blazed across the Mesopotamian sky. Comet Hale-Bopp appeared in Earth's night sky for the first time in 2213 BCE and lingered visibly overhead for eighteen months.

In Mesopotamia—and across much of the ancient world—what followed was a relentless, devastating drought. Rainfall plummeted, and this dry spell was no passing bad season; it dragged on for centuries, leaving a scar across the globe. Climate historians link this same arid crisis to the collapse of Egypt's Old Kingdom and the decline of the Indus Valley civilization.

Extended drought ended Mesopotamia's age of grain surpluses, emptying northern towns and unraveling Sargon's empire.

With year after year of scarce rain, Mesopotamia's golden age of food surpluses came to an abrupt end. Towns and cities in the drier north began to empty out. When King Shar-Kali-Sharri died in 2193 BCE, the empire tumbled into bitter civil war and chaos.

The prolonged drought also pushed a nomadic mountain people from the north—the Guti—down into the Mesopotamian plains. They swept into the weakened heartland and burned Sargon's proud capital of Akkad so thoroughly that archaeologists have never found its ruins. For the next hundred and fifty years, the Guti would hold Mesopotamia in a bleak, fractured dark age.

History still held one final act for the Sumerians. Once the long shadow of the Gutian dark age lifted, they would rise again to lead a brief, radiant renaissance across the valley. Yet the very environment that had once birthed their civilization was already turning against them—slowly, relentlessly preparing to reclaim the land and every great city that had ruled it for ages.

title: Ur and Lagash: Sumer's City-States in an Age of Trade and War
body:
A New Age of Trade and Warfare

In the year 1614 CE, an Italian nobleman named Pietro Della Valle left Venice and sailed to Constantinople. His travels carried him through Turkey, Egypt, and Syria before he reached Iraq in October 1616. In Baghdad, he fell in love with Sitti Maani, an Assyrian Christian noblewoman, and married her within a few months.

In early 1617, while traveling with his new wife and local guides, the party spotted local tribesmen on the distant horizon. Fearing trouble, their guides searched for a place to take cover. In the distance, they made out a sprawling cluster of enormous ruins. While the guides negotiated safe passage with a nearby tribal leader, Della Valle and his companions sheltered among the ruins for several days.

In short

  • Ur's maritime golden age: Positioned where the Euphrates met the sea, Ur forged bronze from imported copper and tin, traded with the Indus Valley, and amassed legendary wealth captured on the Standard of Ur.
  • The birth of organized warfare: Around 2500 BCE, the slaving city of Lagash shattered millennia of relative peace, memorializing its slaughter of Umma on the brutal Stele of the Vultures.
  • Revenge and the Akkadian dawn: Umma's rebel king Lugal-zage-si burned Lagash and claimed the land “between the seas,” only to overstretch his realm and clear the path for Sargon of Akkad.

Pietro Della Valle: First Encounter with Sumerian Ruins

During the day, Della Valle passed the hours wandering among those monumental remains. He would later write:

“Our removal hence being still deferred, I went in the forenoon to take a more diligent view of the ruins of above said ancient building. What it had been, I could not understand. But I have found it have been built with very good bricks, most of which were stamped with certain unknown letters, which appeared very ancient.”

Della Valle was transfixed by the broken fragments of writing scattered across the ground, stamped again and again into stone and clay brick alike. Of these curious marks, he wrote further:

“Amongst other symbols which I discovered in that short time, two I find in many places, one resembled a pyramid while other had a head with seven stars. It looked like they were some kind of seal.”

Bricks stamped with mysterious wedge-shaped letters at Ur gave seventeenth-century Europe its first glimpse of Sumerian writing.

A few days later, once the guides had secured safe passage, Della Valle's party moved on. When he left, he carried several of those cuneiform tablets with him. For the first time, Europeans were being directly introduced to the ancient writing system forged by the Sumerians in the fourth millennium BCE.

The City of Ur: The Port That Forged Bronze

At the time, Della Valle could not have known that the ruins he had explored were those of the ancient Sumerian city of Ur—its identification would not be confirmed until 1815. By the middle of the third millennium BCE, Ur had replaced Uruk as the beating heart of Sumerian civilization.

In the fourth millennium BCE, the epicenter of Sumer had been the great walled city of Uruk. Sitting at the convergence of rivers and canal networks, Uruk was the world's first true metropolis. Its formidable walls and surging population made it the region's de facto leader. Yet Uruk's rise sent ripples far beyond its borders, and as the fourth millennium drew to a close, rival cities of comparable grandeur began to rise around it.

Where the Euphrates once met the Persian Gulf, Ur grew into Mesopotamia's premier maritime gateway.

Among them, Ur gradually supplanted Uruk as the center of Mesopotamia in the opening centuries of the third millennium BCE. It would flourish into realms of untold wealth, pushing the boundaries of what humanity thought possible.

Ur stood right where the Euphrates River met the sea. It was a bustling trading port and fishing town where seagulls wheeled overhead and fishermen bartered their catches—fish, oysters, and turtles—along its docks. Straddling both river and coast made Ur the booming hub of regional commerce. If you needed clay or reeds, southern Iraq had them in abundance; for virtually everything else, the Sumerians had to trade.

Blessed with fertile silt and sophisticated irrigation, the Sumerians harvested rich surpluses year after year. Alone among the peoples of the ancient Middle East, they produced both abundance and extraordinary variety. Archaeologists argue that ancient Mesopotamia enjoyed a far richer and more diverse diet than not only its contemporaries, but even some later Bronze Age civilizations. That culinary richness survives on clay tablets, including ancient Sumerian recipes. One recipe for a stew called Tuh’u captures the flavors they savored:

“Get the water ready, add fat, salt, beer, onion, rocket, coriander, semolina, cumin and beetroot. Add them to the cooking pot, then pound leek and garlic together and add water. Let all blend and reduce to a pulp, then sprinkle with coriander and carrot.”

Boats from Ur: A New Age of Global Trade

Boats laden with wheat and grain, dried reeds, and figs now sailed upriver, carrying food to neighboring lands. In return, prized resources flowed back toward Sumer.

For ordinary construction, timber could be felled in the Zagros Mountains. For finer work—palaces and ornate city gates—only the fragrant wood of the cedar tree would do. Cedar was shipped from the high mountain passes of Lebanon. In The Epic of Gilgamesh, one famous episode even recounts the “king’s quest to slay a monster in the mountains of Lebanon and steal the sacred trees it guarded.”

Silver floated down the Euphrates on barges from Turkey's Taurus Mountains, while gold arrived overland from Egypt and by sea from India. Copper came down from the mountains of northwestern Iran and later by ship from the island of Cyprus. Tin traveled along the rugged mountain passes of Afghanistan, as it would throughout the Bronze Age.

Here in Ur, copper and tin were first alloyed into bronze—a technology that would define the next epoch of human history. In the centuries that followed, Ur remained central to the Bronze Age world as the primary port through which tin flowed.

The Sumerians traded on a scale we would recognize today as truly globalized. From their narrow coast on the Persian Gulf, ships sailed out to ports in modern Bahrain and Oman. From there, they hugged the shoreline eastward to trade with another enigmatic civilization—the people of the Indus Valley in northern India. At the height of Ur's power, the Indus Valley Civilization was entering its mature Harappan phase.

From those distant trading partners of the Indus Valley, Sumerians acquired spices and gemstones of every kind. The brilliant blue lapis lazuli they adored was quarried and routed through the trade networks linked to the Indus Valley cities. Sumerian artisans fashioned it into jewelry, amulets, gaming-board inlays, musical instruments, and sculptures of astonishing beauty.

All of that commerce funneled through Ur, swelling the city to a level of wealth no human settlement had ever achieved before. Grave goods unearthed from the tombs of Ur's kings and ordinary citizens alike reveal not only the staggering riches of its rulers, but also a level of craftsmanship that speaks to a thriving, sophisticated community of artists.

One artifact recovered from a royal tomb in Ur offers an extraordinary window into the lives and manners of the ancient Sumerians: an ornate, box-like piece of decorative furniture inlaid with a mosaic of shell, red limestone, and lapis lazuli.

The Standard of Ur captures Sumerian society in vivid mosaic—chariots and spears on its War panel, farmers, feasts, and scribes on its Peace panel.

Today we call it “The Standard of Ur.” Its panels depict intricate scenes from everyday life. On one side, Sumerians march to war: chariots pulled by donkeys, soldiers in reed skirts and leather helmets, men gripping long spears and battle-axes. On the other side, Sumerians gather in peace: farmers and herders laboring on one register, and above them shaved-headed scribes seated at their desks.

Urbanism in the Sumerian world was reaching its zenith. By the late third millennium BCE, the majority of Sumer's population lived in cities. In this newly urbanized landscape, Ur's economic might remained unmatched. Over the ensuing centuries its political reach expanded and contracted; at one point, Ur's rulers even styled themselves “King of Ur and King of Kish,” claiming authority over a major rival city to the north.

Lagash: The Rise of Warfare and Terror

For more than three thousand years, Sumer had thrived through farming, trade, and shared belief, largely spared from large-scale warfare. By the mid-third millennium BCE, however, Ur's influence began to wane. A harsher, more militarized era was dawning—one in which trade and diplomacy were no longer enough. In this new age of violence, a city named Lagash came into its own.

Lagash was a slaving city. It had grown wealthy by raiding hill villages, kidnapping captives, and selling them across the region. Sometime around 2500 BCE, Lagash clashed with its neighbor, the city of Umma, over a disputed stretch of farmland along the river. The quarrel erupted into war, and one carved stone monument from that conflict—the “Stele of the Vultures”—captures the brutal spirit of the age.

Its upper register looks conventional enough: King Eannatum of Lagash rides ahead of his troops in a chariot, a quiver of spears and javelins at his side, an animal skin draped across his torso. Below, however, Eannatum leads a tight phalanx of soldiers armed with short and long spears straight into a scene of merciless carnage.

The fighting was savage; inscriptions claim that more than four thousand men fell in the battle. As the defeated soldiers of Umma tried to flee, the stele shows Lagash's warriors cutting them down and trampling them underfoot. The monument is unflinching in its portrayal of slaughter.

The Stele of the Vultures—named for the birds of prey carrying away the severed heads of Umma's dead—marks a chilling shift toward terror and imperial conquest.

Something in this carving signals a profound shift in the human mindset of the era. A cruelty that revels in the suffering of enemies appears most starkly in the detail that gave the monument its name: vultures wheeling overhead, gripping the severed heads of fallen Umma soldiers in their beaks and picking at their tongues and eyes. It does not merely record a massacre perpetrated by Lagash—it celebrates it with relish.

After three millennia of growth built on irrigation, commerce, and shared ritual, Sumer was crossing an irreversible threshold into an age of conquest. Powered by its military machine, the slaving city of Lagash went on to subjugate much of southern Mesopotamia. Many historians regard it as the first true empire of the ancient world.

Lugal-zage-si: An Empire Built on Revenge

In that distant age, governing even a single city was daunting. For all its battlefield triumphs, the empire of Lagash was dangerously overstretched. King Eannatum held his short-lived dominion together through campaigns of terror—and, unsurprisingly, revolts soon flared across Sumer.

As the hated empire of Lagash fractured and collapsed, a rebel from one of its conquered cities seized his moment. His name was Lugal-zage-si, and he was the ruler of Umma—the very city whose defeat and humiliation had been carved with such glee onto the Stele of the Vultures. We do not know every secret of Lugal-zage-si's military success, but there is no doubt what drove him: a burning thirst for vengeance against Lagash.

Rising in rebellion, he swiftly toppled the kings still loyal to Lagash in Kish and Larsa. Next, he marched on the great port of Ur and the mighty walled fortress of Uruk. Both fell, and the rebel king moved his capital to Uruk. Finally, he turned on Lagash itself—and there his fiery vengeance burst out in full fury. The city did not hold out for long. Lugal-zage-si stormed over its walls, sacked the city, and burned it to the ground. Even by the harsh standards of the era, it was a shocking act, mourned in horror across several surviving epics.

Driven by vengeance for Umma's humiliation, Lugal-zage-si stormed Lagash and forged a sweeping—if fleeting—Sumerian realm.

After sacking Lagash, Lugal-zage-si's momentum seemed unstoppable. Pressing north along the course of the two rivers, he soon claimed every territory Lagash had once controlled. At the height of his reign, he even boasted of conquering all the land between the Lower Sea and the Upper Sea—meaning the Persian Gulf and the Mediterranean. One of his inscriptions declares:

“The great god Enlil gave kingship of the land to him. The region from the lower sea through the Tigris and Euphrates to the upper sea. Thirty-two kings gathered against him, but he defeated them and smote their cities, prostrated their lords, and destroyed the whole countrysides as far as the silver mines.”

That boast was almost certainly an exaggeration. Up to this point, the Sumerians had never been able to hold distant colonies or occupy far-off territories for long. More likely, Lugal-zage-si led a bold raiding expedition toward the Mediterranean coast, plundering cities and hauling their treasure back to Uruk.

Still, this was the first time any Sumerian prince had ever made such a claim: lordship over the land between the seas. To the Sumerians, the Upper Sea marked the western edge of the known world. The vision of a single monarch uniting all the lands between the two seas planted a seed that would haunt the imagination of every ambitious king who followed him.

Sargon of Akkad: Twilight of the Sumerian Age

Like King Eannatum before him, Lugal-zage-si fell into the trap of overstretching his resources. His realm was simply too vast to hold together. Before long, civil wars and rebellions erupted across Sumer's cities.

As Sumerian city-states tore one another apart, Sargon of Akkad stepped into the breach to usher in a new imperial era.

Into that chaos stepped the other great people of Mesopotamia, sensing their moment to rule. These were the Akkadians—for three thousand years the junior partners of Mesopotamian civilization, living alongside and under Sumerian culture and kings. Soon, one man would lead them into open rebellion against the Sumerian order.

He would go down in history as “Sargon,” a name meaning “the true king” in Akkadian—and he would usher in the twilight of the Sumerian age. Sargon was also a fierce nationalist: he appointed Akkadian officials to run his administration and made Akkadian the official language of his new empire. As the Bronze Age world grew ever more interconnected, Sumerian speech and custom slowly receded, gradually overtaken by Akkadian scripts and culture.

The two peoples of Mesopotamia had been bilingual since antiquity, yet with each passing generation, fewer and fewer Akkadians needed to learn Sumerian—and eventually, even Sumerians themselves stopped speaking it in daily life. Two peoples who had shared the land between the rivers in quiet coexistence since the dawn of history were beginning to drift apart.

The city of Ur would fall and rise countless times over the centuries that followed. Right at the close of the third millennium BCE, it would even surge back to lead a brilliant Sumerian renaissance after a dark age under the Guti. And though Sumerian eventually vanished from everyday speech, it survived for another two thousand years inside temples and ziggurats, revered as the sacred language of the gods.

In the end, it was nature itself—the very force that had birthed this great city—that sealed its final downfall.

The proud port Ur once guarded has vanished without a trace. When archaeologists finally identified the city in 1815 CE, the harbor that had poured boundless wealth through its gates was gone. In the four thousand years since Ur's golden age, relentless deposits of silt and clay carried down by the Tigris and Euphrates have pushed the Persian Gulf coastline nearly 150 kilometers farther south. When explorers first stood among Ur's desert ruins in 1815, they were astonished to find ancient seashells still resting against its walls.

*Note: Paul Cooper’s “Fall of Civilizations” podcast—which formed the inspiration for this series—dates Della Valle’s visit to the ruins of Ur to June 1625.

title: Uruk, the First Metropolis: Where Writing Began
body:
The First Metropolis Where Humans Found Their First Letters

Uruk rose from the clay plains of southern Mesopotamia to become humanity's first great metropolis.

“He who saw the Deep, the foundation of the land,
who knew the ways, was wise in all things.”

So begins The Epic of Gilgamesh—a tale of kingship, grief, immortality, and a flood that once swallowed the world. Composed around 2800 BCE, it is the oldest surviving piece of literature in human history. Its central figure is Gilgamesh, a king of Uruk who had risen to semi-divine stature even before the poem was set down. The city at the heart of the epic, Uruk, would go on to become the cultural and political center of Sumerian civilization in the fourth millennium BCE.

In short

  • The first true metropolis: By the mid-fourth millennium BCE, Uruk surpassed Eridu to become a city of over 50,000 people, powered by secular kingship, mass-produced pottery, and river trade.
  • The birth of writing: Around 3200 BCE, clay and cut reeds came together in Uruk to create cuneiform—transforming accounting lists of barley and beer into humanity's first permanent memory.
  • Everyday Sumer: Behind Uruk's kiln-fired walls and glowing White Temple lay smoky alleys, thirty varieties of beer, drinking songs, sharp inequality, and the earliest industrial workshops.

The Rise of the First Metropolis

As sea levels stabilized around 5000 BCE, the southern coastlines of Mesopotamia began to change. What had once been coastal marshes gradually turned into salt flats. Meanwhile, farther north, Uruk—strategically located near the convergence of rivers and canals—began to thrive. Long before it became the setting of the world's first great epic, Uruk was quietly replacing Eridu as the spiritual and economic center of Sumer. The verses of Gilgamesh would come later, in an age when kings were mythologized and floods became metaphors.

In the fourth millennium BCE, power began to shift across the city-states. Where priests had once governed city life, clan leaders and emerging kings now ruled. The era that followed—known as the Uruk period, named after the city itself—saw the rise of city-states led by secular rulers. By the middle of the fourth millennium BCE, Uruk had grown into one of the largest and most influential cities in Mesopotamia, with a population of over 50,000—larger than any city the world had yet seen.

Archaeologists now link the drastic stylistic shift in pottery during this time with the cultural handover from Eridu to Uruk. Pottery from the earlier Ubaid and Eridu periods was refined and handsome, crafted on the slow wheel and painted with intricate geometric patterns. Those vessels were expensive and used primarily by elites.

In Uruk, potters developed a new technique: the fast wheel. It enabled mass production to meet the demands of a rapidly growing population—though at the expense of craftsmanship. Yet even as pottery lost its elegance, daily life improved in other ways. For the first time in human history, people were no longer limited to eating only what they produced themselves. Boats navigated the rivers and canals, carrying food and goods from neighboring regions. During this period, Sumerians also began venturing far beyond their homeland—into Babylonia, Elam, and even the Anatolian and European highlands.

All of this took place more than five thousand years ago. By then, Sumerian civilization was already two thousand years old—a span of time as long as the centuries separating us from Julius Caesar. Yet the first Egyptian pyramids would not rise for another nine centuries, and the first stones of Stonehenge would not be set in place for another thirteen hundred years.

The First Light of History: Writing Is Born (3200 BCE)

When gas clouds compacted by their own weight build enough pressure and gravity, the first stars burst into being. When enough people gather in one place, a settlement develops a gravity of its own—drawing still more people toward it. As the size of a settlement increases, so does the pressure on its systems. By the middle of the fourth millennium BCE, as Uruk expanded into a true metropolis, its population density—and the sheer complexity of its daily interactions—gave rise to an even more intricate form of human organization.

The first stars of human settlement burst into light in Uruk sometime around 3200 BCE. A later Sumerian epic, Enmerkar and the Lord of Aratta, attributes the invention of writing to the “Lord of Kullaba,” a king overwhelmed by too many messages for his courier to hold in memory:

“Because the messenger’s mouth was heavy and he couldn’t repeat the message,
the Lord of Kullaba patted some clay and put words on it like a tablet.
Until then, there had been no putting words on clay.”

The Sumerians had two things in abundance: clay beneath their feet, and reeds growing thick along the riverbanks. Together, they formed humanity's first writing system. Scribes would pat a lump of wet clay into roughly the size of a modern smartphone, cut a reed into a wedge, and press it into the surface to leave crisp impressions. Those distinctive wedge shapes gave the script its name: cuneiform.

Pressed into damp river clay with a cut reed, early cuneiform turned everyday ration tallies into humanity's first written records.

The earliest cuneiform signs were pictographs—simple images depicting everyday objects so that anyone could read them at a glance. A fish meant fish. A scratched circle stood for a head of cattle. A jar symbolized oil. Initially, these signs were used to keep track of supplies, taxes, and rations. This pictographic system, known as proto-cuneiform, emerged around 3300 BCE. Its first records may have been dry—lists of goats, measures of barley, allocations of beer—but their implications were monumental.

The oldest excavated cuneiform tablet dates to around 3200 BCE. It depicts a bowl of food with an eating mouth beside six impressions, and a sheaf of wheat beside five—indicating that a worker could exchange the tablet for six bowls of food or five sheaves of wheat. Scribes would have had to work swiftly, turning out hundreds of such documents every day.

Over time, these pictographs grew simpler and more abstract as scribes invented shortcuts and standardized their strokes. Before long, the signs no longer resembled the objects they represented. By the start of the third millennium BCE, the inventory of signs had shrunk from more than 1,500 to around 600. Around the same time, someone had a brilliant idea: each symbol could stand for a specific sound rather than an entire object or concept. That leap laid the foundation for phonetic writing—the earliest step toward an alphabet.

With this innovation, however, came exclusivity. Only an educated class of scribes could decipher the new signs, and a specialized profession was born. The human mind would never be the same. For the first time, knowledge could outlive speech and memory.

As the clay dried, those letters remained etched into history. That is why we can still play Sumerian music and read Sumerian epics today. People could hear and read the words of kings and scribes who had died centuries before. Authority could now be transferred across distance and generations, not merely spoken aloud. Just as importantly, people could record everything they had learned so that it would not only be remembered, but built upon. Partly because of this newfound capacity to accumulate knowledge, Sumerian technology would take even greater leaps in the next phase of its history.

Walls, Temples, and the Rhythm of Daily Life

By 3000 BCE, Uruk stood as the epicenter of Sumerian administration, agriculture, and ritual. Its scribes had etched thousands of tablets. Its merchants ferried goods across rivers and marshes. Its temples functioned simultaneously as banks, warehouses, and courts of law.

It is in this city that The Epic of Gilgamesh opens—the world's oldest literary work. Its hero, two-thirds god and one-third man, may well have been a real king who ruled Uruk around 2700 BCE.

Though the epic is more myth than chronicle, it reveals how deeply life in Uruk was changing in the early third millennium BCE. For one, warfare was beginning to intensify across the region, and city-states now needed walls. In the poem, Uruk's fortifications are celebrated with fierce pride, hailed again and again as “Strong-Walled Uruk.” The narrator calls out:

“Go up on the wall of Uruk and walk around,
examine its foundation, inspect its brickwork thoroughly.
Is not even the core of the structure made of kiln-fired brick?
Did not the Seven Sages themselves lay out its plan?”

— The Epic of Gilgamesh, Tablet I

The epic also gives us a glimpse of how the city was partitioned, hinting at deliberate urban planning by its rulers:

“These parts comprise Uruk:
one third for the city,
one third for garden,
one third for field and the precinct for the temple of Ishtar.”

Uruk had a bustling port on the river, lined with workshops and tightly packed houses. Rising at the center of it all was Uruk's famed White Temple of Ishtar—elevated twenty-one meters above the plain and coated in white plaster so that it gleamed brilliantly in the desert sun. At the height of the Uruk period, the city spanned 2.5 square kilometers and housed more than 50,000 people.

At the heart of Uruk's maze of mudbrick alleys rose its elevated temple precinct, visible for miles across the plain.

In the wealthier quarters of town, homes were constructed from baked brick; elsewhere, they were built of sun-dried clay. Affluent neighborhoods featured houses with intricate arches and domes. Inside, residents laid down layers of clay, crushed gypsum dust, and reed matting to create a smooth, carpet-like floor. At night, families routinely slept on their rooftops, escaping the stifling heat trapped inside the mudbrick rooms.

The city itself would have assaulted the senses with a pungent mixture of smells. Pottery kilns and brickworks belched smoke throughout the day. There was no drainage system, and residents tossed their household refuse directly into the streets. Houses clustered together chaotically, forming a labyrinth of narrow alleys draped overhead with reed matting to shade passersby from the blistering midday sun.

Beer, Laments, and the Dawn of Mass Production

Walk down the streets of Uruk in that era and you would pass stalls piled high with lentils and beans, pomegranates and dates, and clay jars brimming with syrup and oil. Farmers trudged by carrying heavy bundles of reeds and wheat on their backs. Herders drove long-haired sheep and oxen through the gates. In shaded courtyards, men gathered in circles around a single large jar of beer set in the center, sipping it together through straws made from hollow reeds. Although the Sumerians knew how to make wine, it was beer they loved above all else.

Brewed directly from wheat and millet, Sumerian beer came in more than thirty distinct varieties—pale, dark, cloudy, infused with herbs, or sweetened with honey. The cheaper brews still had bits of grain floating on the surface. One cuneiform tablet from the early third millennium BCE preserves one of their drinking songs:

“I will summon brewers and cupbearers to serve us floods of beer and pass it around.
What pleasure! What delight!
Blissfully to take it in.
To sing jubilantly of this noble liquor.
Our hearts are enchanted and our souls radiant.”

Just as tablets recorded details of Sumerian musical instruments, they also captured the everyday conversations of ordinary people. From those clay records, we can eavesdrop on what citizens talked about in their courtyards and taverns over shared jars of beer—and their worries feel unmistakably familiar.

On one tablet, a frustrated man laments: “I am a thoroughbred steed, but I am hitched to a mule.” Life for the poor was harsh, often forcing families to borrow food and silver from predatory lenders. Another cuneiform tablet captures their quiet despair: “The poor man is better dead than alive; if he has bread, he has no salt; if he has salt, he has no water.”

Because coined money did not yet exist, workers were paid directly in food and essential goods. The minimum ration for an unskilled laborer was twenty liters of barley per month, supplemented by two liters of oil and two kilos of wool per year. Supervisors earned twice as much.

This era also marked the dawn of mass production. Sumerian clay tablets paint a vivid portrait of a booming industrial economy. In the city of Girsu, for example, fifteen thousand women were employed in the textile industry. One large workshop produced eleven hundred tons of flour a year, along with bread, beer, and linseed oil—employing 134 specialists and 858 skilled workers, the vast majority of them women.

From bustling workshops and shared jars of beer to maritime ambition, Uruk's urban experiment reshaped the ancient world.

Beyond Uruk: The Road to Ur and the Bronze Age

Uruk's transformation sent ripples far across the ancient world, inspiring rival cities to rise around it. As the third millennium BCE unfolded, one of those Sumerian neighbors—Ur—gradually surpassed Uruk in power and prestige. Positioned where river met sea, Ur would emerge as a hub of maritime trade and a beacon of art and architecture. The world was stepping into the Bronze Age, and Sumer's legacy was about to sail farther than its rivers had ever flowed.
